entry: Scottish Franciscan friar, philosopher and theologian of the late Middle Ages. Scotus is considered, with [[Thomas Aquinas]], [[Bonaventure]] and [[William of Ockham]], one of the most important philosopher-theologians of Western Christendom in that period. He was given the scholastic title *Doctor Subtilis* ("the subtle Doctor"). His best-known doctrines include the "univocity of being," the view that existence is the most abstract concept, applicable to everything that exists; the formal distinction; and haecceity, the property that makes each thing an individual. He also developed a complex argument for the existence of God and argued for the Immaculate Conception of Mary. Scotus is traditionally said to have studied at [[Oxford]], and he lectured at Paris until he was expelled for siding with [[Pope Boniface VIII]] against [[Philip IV of France|Philip IV]] over the taxation of church property. He was beatified by [[Pope John Paul II]] in 1993.

English pop rock band formed in [[Birmingham]] in 1978. One of the leading bands of the New Romantic scene in the early 1980s, the group was an innovator of the [[Music video|music video]] and a major act in the [[MTV]]-driven Second British Invasion of the US. In 1985 the single "A View to a Kill," from the soundtrack of a [[James Bond]] film, topped the U.S. charts. The band was inducted into the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]] in 2022.

Port city (pop., 2011: 595,061), on the east coast of South Africa. Durban is the busiest port city in sub-Saharan Africa and the largest city in [[KwaZulu-Natal]] province. Its beaches and warm climate make it a popular tourist destination. [[Vasco da Gama]] sighted the coast during [[Christmas]] 1497 and named it Natal, the Portuguese word for Christmas. English traders established a trading post at Port Natal in 1824, and in 1835 the settlement was named Durban after Sir Benjamin D'Urban, governor of the Cape Colony. Indentured laborers from British India arrived from 1860 onward. Durban was granted city status in 1935 and was one of the host cities of the 2010 FIFA World Cup. It is [[UNESCO]]'s first City of Literature in Africa.

Major goddess in [[Hinduism]], associated with protection, strength, motherhood and war. Believed to have originated as a goddess of indigenous mountain-dwellers, Durga was established in the main Hindu pantheon by the 4th century CE. She is widely worshipped by followers of [[Shaktism]], which regards her as the principal aspect of Mahadevi, the Ultimate Reality. Usually depicted as a warrior with many arms riding a lion or tiger, she is best known for slaying the buffalo demon Mahishasura. In Vaishnava contexts she is revered as a female form of [[Vishnu]]; in later traditions she became associated with [[Shiva]]. In [[Bengal]] she is considered the mother of Ganesha, Kartikeya, Lakshmi and Sarasvati. Durga is mostly worshipped after the spring and autumn harvests, especially during Durga Puja and Navaratri, across [[Nepal]], [[India]] and Bangladesh.

Edible fruit of trees in the genus *Durio*, most often *Durio zibethinus*, the only species available on the international market. Known in some regions as the "king of fruits," the durian is distinctive for its large size, strong odor and thorn-covered rind. The fruit typically weighs 1 to 3 kg. Its creamy, pudding-like flesh has a complex, savory flavor and ranges from pale yellow to red, depending on the species. Its strong smell, which may linger for several days, has led some hotels and public transportation services in [[Singapore]] and [[Bangkok]] to ban the fruit. The flesh is used to flavor sweet desserts and savory dishes across Southeast Asian cuisines, and the seeds can be eaten when cooked. Durian flowers are large, feathery and rich in nectar, typical of flowers pollinated by [[Bat|bats]].

Period of severe dust storms and drought on the [[Great Plains]], 1930–1940. Severe drought and the destruction of topsoil by settlers who did not use dryland farming methods to prevent wind erosion greatly damaged agriculture and ecology in western [[Kansas]], the Oklahoma and Texas panhandles, and parts of [[Colorado]] and [[New Mexico]]. The drought came in waves in 1934, 1936 and 1939–1940. The period inspired [[John Steinbeck]]'s novels *Of Mice and Men* and *The Grapes of Wrath*, and the ballads of [[Woody Guthrie]].

Fine particles of solid matter, suspended in the air or settled on surfaces. On Earth, atmospheric dust comes mainly from soil lifted by wind, from volcanic eruptions and from pollution. When fine particles remain suspended for an extended time, dust is considered an [[Aerosol]]. Dust in homes and offices is composed of about 20–50% dead skin [[Cell (biology)|cells]], along with pollen, human hair, animal fur, textile and paper fibers, and minerals from outdoor soil. Dust-producing surfaces cover one-third of the global land area, roughly 13 billion hectares, and [[Sahara|Saharan]] dust can be transported as far as the [[Caribbean]] and the Amazon basin, where it may affect air temperature and rainfall. Total suspended dust concentrations range from 0.01 to 10,000 mg/m³ in outdoor settings such as residential, industrial and commercial areas, highways and quarries.

Meteorological phenomenon in which strong wind lifts loose sand and dirt from dry surfaces, common in arid and semi-arid regions. Also called a sandstorm, a dust storm can reduce visibility, disrupt transportation and pose serious health risks. Gust fronts from thunderstorms can trigger storms, as can dry cold fronts, which were common during the [[Dust Bowl]] years. Drought, poor farming and grazing practices, and wildfires also contribute. Fine particles travel by saltation and suspension, and repeated storms can reduce agricultural productivity and contribute to desertification. The arid regions of [[North Africa]], the [[Middle East]], [[Central Asia]] and [[China]] are the main terrestrial sources of airborne dust, and it has been argued that poor management of drylands, such as neglecting the fallow system, is increasing the size and frequency of storms.

American actor and filmmaker, one of the key leading men in the formation of [[New Hollywood]]. He won two [[Academy Awards]] for Best Actor, for *Kramer vs. Kramer* (1979) and *Rain Man* (1988). He was also Oscar-nominated for *The Graduate* and *Tootsie*. Hoffman won a Primetime Emmy Award for reprising the role of Willy Loman in *Death of a Salesman*, and in 2012 he made his directorial debut with *Quartet*.

British singer of blue-eyed soul, pop and dramatic ballads. Born in West Hampstead, London, she became an icon of the Swinging Sixties. Her solo career began in 1963 with "I Only Want to Be with You," the first of six transatlantic top 40 hits of the 1960s. Her 1968 album *Dusty in Memphis* includes "Son of a Preacher Man," and in 1987 her collaboration with [[Pet Shop Boys]] reached No. 2 in the UK and the US. She was inducted into the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]].

Chartered Dutch trading company, among the first joint-stock companies in the world. Established on 20 March 1602 by the States General of the Netherlands, it held a 21-year monopoly on trade in Asia and had quasi-governmental powers, including the ability to wage war and negotiate treaties. Shares could be bought and sold in open-air secondary markets, one of which became the [[Amsterdam]] Stock Exchange. Between 1602 and 1796 the company sent nearly one million Europeans to Asia on 4,785 ships. It enjoyed huge profits from its spice monopoly through most of the 17th century and paid annual dividends that averaged about 18% of capital for almost 200 years. It founded a capital at Jayakarta in 1619, renamed Batavia, now [[Jakarta]]. Weighed down by smuggling, corruption and administrative costs, the company went bankrupt and was dissolved in 1799.

Dutch colony in Southeast Asia, now mostly [[Indonesia]]. Established in 1800, when the Batavian Republic took control of the [[Dutch East India Company]], the colony expanded through 19th-century wars against indigenous states. It contributed to Dutch prominence in spice and cash crop trade in the 19th century and in coal and oil exploration in the 20th. The colonial social order was rigidly racial. Japan's occupation during [[World War II]] dismantled much of the colonial state and economy. After Japan surrendered in August 1945, Indonesian nationalists [[Sukarno]] and Hatta declared independence. The Dutch deployed roughly 220,000 troops against the nationalists before recognizing Indonesian sovereignty at the 1949 Dutch–Indonesian Round Table Conference. In 1962 the Dutch turned over their last possession, Western New Guinea, to Indonesia, and the colony ceased to exist.

Period of Dutch history, from 1588 to 1672, of maritime and commercial prosperity. The Dutch Republic became one of the leading commercial and maritime powers in Europe, with a large merchant fleet and a strong presence in international trade, particularly through [[Amsterdam]]. The Republic also helped develop modern financial practices, including stock exchange trading, joint-stock companies and public debt markets. The [[Dutch East India Company]] helped extend the Republic's reach in global commerce. Dutch culture flourished. Skilled Protestant craftsmen and merchants migrated north from the southern Netherlands, transforming Amsterdam from a small harbor into one of the world's most important ports by 1630. The Republic gained formal independence from Spain under the [[Peace of Westphalia]] in 1648. Because of Dutch involvement in slavery and colonialism, the term has been controversial, and several museums in the Netherlands have deprecated it.

West Germanic language of the Indo-European family, spoken natively by about 25 million people, chiefly in the [[Netherlands]] and [[Flanders]]. Dutch was one of the official languages of South Africa until 1925, when it was replaced by [[Afrikaans]], a separate but partially mutually intelligible language that evolved from Cape Dutch dialects. It is the native language of the majority of the population of Suriname and an official language of Aruba, Curaçao and Sint Maarten. In the [[Dutch East Indies]], Dutch was used by a limited educated elite of about 2% of the population. About a fifth of the [[Indonesian language]] can be traced to Dutch, including many loan words. Dutch is one of the closest relatives of German and English. Like English, it has not undergone the High German consonant shift, and it has largely abandoned the subjunctive and leveled much of its morphology.

Small [[Galaxy|galaxy]] composed of about 1,000 to several billion stars, compared with 100–400 billion in the [[Milky Way]]. Dwarf galaxies are classified by shape and composition into types including dwarf elliptical, dwarf spheroidal, dwarf irregular and blue compact dwarf galaxies. Their formation and activity are thought to be heavily influenced by interactions with larger galaxies. Dwarf galaxies in the [[Local Group]] frequently orbit larger galaxies such as the Milky Way, the [[Andromeda Galaxy]] and the [[Triangulum Galaxy]]. Astronomers believe that [[Omega Centauri]], the largest globular cluster in the Milky Way, is the core of a dwarf galaxy. Around 30–50% of dwarf galaxies in low-density environments are quenched, meaning they have little star formation.

Small planetary-mass object in direct orbit around the Sun, massive enough to be gravitationally rounded but insufficient to achieve orbital dominance. The prototypical dwarf planet is [[Pluto]], which was regarded as a planet for decades before the category was adopted in 2006. Since then the International Astronomical Union and many astronomers have excluded dwarf planets from the roster of planets, though many planetary geologists consider them planets. Dwarf planets are capable of being geologically active, an expectation borne out in 2015 by the [[New Horizons]] mission to Pluto and the Dawn mission to [[Ceres (dwarf planet)|Ceres]]. At least nine candidates are generally agreed to be dwarf planets: Pluto, [[Eris (dwarf planet)|Eris]], [[Haumea]], [[Makemake]], [[Gonggong (dwarf planet)|Gonggong]], Quaoar, [[Sedna (dwarf planet)|Sedna]], Ceres and Orcus.

Condition marked by unusually small size or short stature, defined in humans as an adult height of 147 cm (4 ft 10 in) or less. Achondroplasia, a genetic disorder, accounts for 70% of cases, and growth hormone deficiency is responsible for most others. Intelligence is usually normal, and most people with dwarfism have a nearly normal life expectancy. Height [[Discrimination|discrimination]] can lead to ridicule in childhood and to discrimination in adulthood, and many [[Support group|support groups]] provide services to aid individuals.

American actor and semi-retired [[Professional wrestling|professional wrestler]], known as "the Rock." Johnson was integral to the development and success of the WWF (now [[WWE]]) during the Attitude Era before becoming one of the world's highest-grossing actors, with films that have grossed over $11.4 billion worldwide. His film roles include the *Fast & Furious* series and *Jumanji: Welcome to the Jungle*, and he voiced Maui in *Moana*. In 2016 and 2019, [[Time (magazine)|Time]] named him one of the world's most influential people.

American Army general and 34th president of the United States (1953–1961). A member of the [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican Party]], he commanded Allied forces in Operation Torch and Operation Overlord during [[World War II]] and attained the five-star rank of General of the Army in 1944. He was the first supreme commander of [[NATO]] and had been president of [[Columbia University]]. He won the 1952 and 1956 presidential elections in landslides, and his main goals in office were to contain communism and reduce federal deficits. An armistice ending the [[Korean War]] was reached in 1953, and his administration developed the [[Interstate Highway System]]. After the Soviet launch of Sputnik, he led the response that created [[NASA]]. In his farewell address he warned of massive military spending, which he dubbed the "[[Military–industrial complex|military–industrial complex]]."

American [[Basketball|basketball]] executive and former professional player. Nicknamed "D-Wade" and "Flash," he spent most of his 16-year career with the [[Miami]] Heat of the [[National Basketball Association]], winning three championships and being a 13-time All-Star. He was named the 2006 NBA Finals MVP and led the United States men's team in scoring at the 2008 Summer Olympics, where it won gold. Wade won the NBA scoring title in the 2008–09 season. He later became a minority owner of the Utah Jazz.

Soluble colored substance, natural or synthetic, used to color textiles and other materials. Unlike [[Pigment|pigments]], which are insoluble, dyes are usually soluble in a solvent and can chemically bind to the material they color. Textile dyeing dates back to the [[Neolithic]] period, and dyed flax fibers from a prehistoric cave in the [[Georgia (country)|Republic of Georgia]] date to 36,000 BP. Scarce natural dyes such as [[Tyrian purple]] were prized luxury items in the ancient and medieval world. The first synthetic dye, *mauveine*, was discovered by William Henry Perkin in 1856, starting a surge in synthetic dyes and in organic chemistry. Most dyes used in the modern world are synthetic, made from petrochemicals, while natural dyes come mainly from plants.

Welsh poet and writer. Born in [[Swansea]], he left school to become a reporter for the *South Wales Daily Post*, and while still a teenager he published poems including "And death shall have no dominion." His best-known works include the poem "Do not go gentle into that good night" and the "play for voices" *Under Milk Wood*. His radio recordings for the [[BBC]] in the late 1940s brought him to a wider public, and his readings in the United States brought him a degree of fame, though his drinking worsened. He fell into a coma during a fourth trip to [[New York City]], and he was buried in Laugharne, Wales. Later appraisals have emphasized his original, rhythmic use of language and his modernist poetics, setting aside the legend of the "doomed poet."

Mathematical optimization method and algorithmic paradigm based on breaking a complex problem into simpler subproblems. Developed by Richard Bellman in the 1950s, it has found applications in fields such as [[Aerospace engineering]] and [[Economics|economics]]. In computer science, a problem has optimal substructure when it can be solved optimally by recursively finding optimal solutions to its subproblems. The relationship between the value of the larger problem and that of its subproblems is called the Bellman equation.

Mathematical model of the time dependence of a point in an ambient space, such as in a parametric curve. Examples include the swinging of a clock [[Pendulum|pendulum]], the flow of water in a pipe and the number of fish in a lake each spring. A dynamical system has a state, often given by a tuple of [[Real number|real numbers]] or by a vector in a manifold, and an evolution rule that describes which future states follow from the current state. The rule is often deterministic, though some systems are stochastic. The most general definition unifies concepts such as [[Ordinary differential equation|ordinary differential equations]] and ergodic theory. The study of dynamical systems is the focus of [[Dynamical systems theory]], and dynamical systems are a fundamental part of [[Chaos theory]].

Area of mathematics describing the long-term qualitative behavior of complex [[Dynamical system|dynamical systems]], usually by employing differential equations or difference equations. When differential equations are used, the theory is called continuous dynamical systems; when difference equations are used, it is called discrete. From a physical point of view, continuous dynamical systems generalize [[Classical mechanics]], in which the equations of motion are postulated directly and need not derive from a least action principle. The field studies systems such as planetary orbits, electronic circuits, and systems in biology and economics. Its central goals include finding the fixed points, or steady states, of a system and determining whether long-term behavior depends on initial conditions. Much modern research focuses on chaotic systems, and the branch that investigates chaos is called [[Chaos theory]].
